definition: In machine learning, the polynomial kernel is a kernel function commonly used with support vector machines (SVMs) and other kernelized models, that represents the similarity of vectors (training samples) in a feature space over polynomials of the original variables, allowing learning of non-linear models.
details: Intuitively, the polynomial kernel looks not only at the given features of input samples to determine their similarity, but also combinations of these. In the context of regression analysis, such combinations are known as interaction features. The (implicit) feature space of a polynomial kernel is equivalent to that of polynomial regression, but without the combinatorial blowup in the number of parameters to be learned. When the input features are binary-valued (booleans), then the features correspond to logical conjunctions of input features.

explainer.lead: The polynomial kernel is a kernel function used with support vector machines and other kernelized models, representing vector similarity over polynomials of the original variables. It allows learning non-linear models without the combinatorial blowup in parameters.

tiers.eli5: Instead of comparing two things only by their raw features, it also compares combinations of features, like comparing pairs as well as singles.
tiers.practitioner: Used in SVMs to capture interaction features implicitly. A pitfall is choosing a high degree, which makes computation costly and risks overfitting.
tiers.paperLevel: The kernel computes similarity as a polynomial of the dot product of the input vectors, typically (a·b + c)^d, with degree d and constant c. Its implicit feature space equals that of polynomial regression but without the parameter blowup; the degree controls capacity and cost.

explainer.example: An SVM with a degree-2 polynomial kernel classifies samples using not just each feature but their pairwise products.
